rows.why: Each internal workflow where AI output drives a decision (HR, finance, approvals, operations) is identified with its purpose, the staff who use it and the decisions it feeds.
The knowledge limits of the AI used in internal workflows, and the conditions where its output must not be relied on, are documented for the staff who act on it.
The cost of an internal decision made on wrong AI output, or of insider misuse of the AI, is examined with its likelihood and magnitude against risk tolerance.
The scope of internal decisions the AI may support, and the uses staff must not put it to, is specified so off-label use and misuse can be recognised.
Staff who act on AI output in internal workflows are trained on its limits, over-reliance and safe data handling, and their proficiency is assessed.
rows.review_reason: LLM-14.5 is off-topic: it is about keeping sensitive data out of unapproved consumer AI web interfaces (shadow AI, the invisible_usage area), not training staff on the limits and over-reliance of the AI in sanctioned internal workflows; it also repeats LLM-14.4's data-handling evidence.

rows.why: Human review and sign-off points for AI-driven internal decisions are defined, with who must check the output before it takes effect.
The accuracy of AI output used in internal workflows is monitored in production against actual outcomes, with alerts when it drifts or becomes unreliable.
The AI is shown to be valid and reliable for the specific internal decision it supports before staff rely on it, with limits of that validation documented.

AI-assisted internal decisions are logged with the user, input, output and any human override, the degree of human oversight is documented, and the logs are reviewed so decisions and insider misuse can be traced to who acted.

AI output that drives internal HR, finance and approval decisions comes with an explanation staff can interpret in context, so they can judge wrong output instead of over-relying on it and decisions about people can be justified.
Privacy risk of personal data (e.g. employee or finance records) processed by AI in internal workflows is examined, including monitoring staff queries for sensitive data access.
AI output used in internal decisions about people, such as HR screening or approvals, is evaluated for bias across affected groups and the results documented.
Staff and people affected by AI-driven internal decisions can report wrong output and appeal outcomes, and those reports feed the evaluation of the AI.

Domain experts and the staff who use the AI in each internal workflow give feedback, including override rates, that is used to validate whether the AI performs consistently as intended there, and the results are documented.
A documented decision is made, and revisited, on whether the AI meets its purpose in each internal workflow and whether its use there should continue.
Business rules, human-in-the-loop steps and data access limits restrict what AI output can decide and which data staff can reach through it in internal workflows.
Someone is assigned and able to stop or bypass the AI in an internal workflow when its output is wrong, with a manual fallback so the process continues.
Wrong decisions and misuse arising from AI in internal workflows are reported, tracked, responded to, rectified and reviewed afterwards, and communicated to those affected.
Where AI code generation may be used is set out: which repositories, codebases and data may be given to a code assistant and which are kept out.
Developers using code assistants are trained on the AI-specific risks: made-up packages, untrusted dependencies and secrets pasted into prompts.
Human review of AI-generated code before it is merged is defined, including who reviews it and what they must check.
The code assistants in use and the third-party packages they introduce are identified, with their source, licence and intellectual-property risk.
The controls around each code assistant are identified, such as approved package registries, secret filtering of prompts and the vendor's retention settings.
Dependencies suggested by AI are checked to exist, come from a trusted source and be free of known vulnerabilities before they are used.
rows.review_reason: The row tests only AI-suggested dependencies; no MEASURE row checks that secrets and credentials are actually kept out of code-assistant prompts (e.g. DLP or secret scanning of prompt traffic, LLM-3.13), one of the area's three core risks, which MAP 4.2 only identifies as a control.

rows.why: Code assistant use is logged and AI-generated changes can be traced to who prompted them and who reviewed them before merge.

Personal data that can reach a code assistant, such as customer records in test fixtures, database extracts, logs or code pasted as context, is examined and documented, with what was sent and how long the vendor keeps it.
New risks from code generation, such as package-squatting campaigns on made-up names or flaws in the assistant itself, are tracked.
There is a followed procedure to respond when a malicious AI-suggested package or a secret leaked through a prompt is found, including removal and credential rotation.
A code assistant can be switched off for a repository or the organisation, with an owner who decides when it misbehaves or leaks.
Third-party code assistants and the packages they pull in are monitored, and unapproved assistants or untrusted packages are removed.
Incidents from AI-generated code, such as leaked secrets or bad dependencies, are recorded, reviewed and communicated to the developers affected.
The purpose of each customer-facing AI application, the public users it serves, what they expect from it and the settings it is deployed in are documented.
The application's knowledge limits, and how customers are told what its answers can and cannot be relied on for and when a human takes over, are documented.
The scope of what the customer-facing AI may answer or do, and the topics and data it must stay out of, is specified and documented.
The controls on the customer-facing application's components, such as input and output guardrails and separation of system instructions from user input, are identified and documented.
The likelihood and impact of public users attacking the application (prompt injection, abuse) and of wrong, harmful or leaked answers reaching customers, including their cost, are identified.
The customer-facing application's behaviour in production is monitored for abuse patterns, adversarial prompting and degraded or unsafe answers.
The accuracy and reliability of answers given to customers are tested before release and checked in use, with known limits recorded.
The application is evaluated for harmful or unsafe output to customers and shown to fail safely when it cannot answer.
The customer-facing application is security tested against prompt injection, jailbreaks, abuse and data extraction by public users, and its resilience is evaluated.
Customer interactions with the AI are logged with inputs, outputs and user attribution, so answers given to customers can be traced and accounted for.
rows.review_reason: The why covers only internal logging of interactions; for a customer-facing application the transparency risk is towards customers (being told they are dealing with AI, explanations of answers, recourse), which no row examines.

rows.why: The application is tested and monitored for answers that leak personal or confidential data to customers.
Answers given to different groups of customers are evaluated for bias and unfair treatment.
Customers can report wrong or harmful answers and appeal outcomes, and those reports feed the application's evaluation.
The residual risks the customer-facing application still poses to customers after controls are documented.

The risk treatments for the customer-facing application are applied and kept effective in operation: business rules that restrict what answers may go out, input and output guardrails, data loss checks on answers, and authentication and throttling of public users against abuse.
There are procedures to respond to and recover from new failures of the customer-facing AI, such as a successful injection or a leaked answer.
The customer-facing AI can be switched off or replaced by a fallback quickly when it behaves unsafely, and who may do so is known.
Incidents and errors in answers to customers are tracked, reviewed and communicated to affected customers and other relevant parties.
For each vendor product with AI features turned on, what the feature does, which of the org's data it processes and where that data flows (the vendor and its model provider) are known and recorded.
The vendor's terms, contracts and documentation are reviewed for how its AI keeps, trains on, shares or relocates the org's data and which model provider sits behind it.
The controls the org relies on for each vendor AI feature (permitted data classifications, training opt-out, retention settings) are identified and documented per vendor.
The vendor's AI security is evaluated before and while it is used, including tenant isolation and how the org's data is separated from other customers'.
Use of vendor AI features on the org's data is logged, using the vendor's admin and audit logs where available, so it can be traced to users and reviewed.
The privacy risk of sending the org's data to vendor AI is examined in use, including whether sensitive or personal data reaches the vendor's model.
Someone is assigned and able to switch off a vendor's AI feature for the org's tenant when it behaves or handles data in ways the org did not accept.
Vendor AI settings are applied and kept (history retention off, training opt-out, risky features disabled) and the vendor is monitored for feature, terms or data-handling changes.
Vendor AI changes go through change management, and when a vendor or its AI feature is dropped the org's data is removed and the vendor's access revoked.
Incidents involving vendor AI, such as a data exposure or unannounced feature change, are reported to and from the vendor, responded to, tracked and recorded.
The intended purpose, users, deployment settings and application scope of each model the org builds or tunes, including for recipients it is released to, are defined and documented.
The task the model supports and the methods used to build it (architecture, training or tuning approach) are defined, with the requirements the design must meet.
The model's knowledge limits and how its output should be used and overseen are documented (e.g. model card) and given to those who receive the model.
Experimental design, training data selection and the TEVV approach for the model are identified and documented before and during building.
The components of the model (base model, datasets, libraries) are recorded with their source, version and license, and their technical, legal and IP risks are mapped.
Controls on the model's components and artifacts, such as integrity checks on base weights, training data and the released model, are identified and documented.
The likelihood and magnitude of harms from the model's errors or misuse, for the org and for recipients, are assessed, including through threat modelling of the model.
People outside the team that built the model, or independent assessors, review its evaluation before it is released or changed.
The test sets, metrics and tools used to evaluate the model are chosen for its main risks, documented, and their effectiveness reviewed.
The released model's behaviour is monitored in production for drift, declines and emergent risks.
The model's performance is measured under conditions like its deployment and shown to be valid and reliable, with limits of generalisation documented.
The model is evaluated for safety before release and after changes, including how it behaves beyond its knowledge limits.
The model's security and resilience (e.g. poisoning, backdoors, extraction, jailbreaks) are tested adversarially and the results documented.
Training and tuning runs, model changes and releases are logged with who made them, so the model's lineage can be traced and accounted for.
The model is explained, validated and documented so its output can be interpreted in context by the org and by recipients.
The model built or tuned is tested before release for whether it memorises and can disclose personal data from its training or tuning data, and the results are documented.
rows.review_reason: Impact is only 'assets', but the row protects personal data in the training or tuning data from being memorised and disclosed; impact should include 'data'.

rows.why: The model is evaluated for bias introduced by its training or tuning data and methods, with results disaggregated across affected groups and documented before release to recipients.
The environmental impact of training and tuning the model is assessed and documented.
Recipients and end users of the model have a way to report problems with it, and those reports feed its evaluation.
A documented go/no-go decision is made on whether the model meets its objectives before it is released or a new version promoted.
The model's unmitigated residual risks are documented for downstream recipients and end users.
There is a way, with assigned owners, to supersede, roll back or withdraw a released model version that behaves inconsistently with intended use.
Base and pre-trained models and other third-party components used to build the model are monitored for vulnerabilities and changes.
Changes to the model after release go through change management with version control, and a post-release monitoring and decommissioning plan is followed.
Updates to the model are driven by measurable improvement goals and by feedback gathered from recipients and other interested parties, with the basis for trade-offs documented.
Incidents and errors in the model are responded to, recovered from and communicated to recipients, with records kept.
AI tools, features, local models, agents and PoCs that staff use without approval are found and recorded with the org data and systems each one reaches.
rows.review_reason: The why is finding and recording unapproved AI (inventory, GOVERN territory, and the same discovery MEASURE 3.1 checks) rather than MAP 4.1's outcome: mapping the technology and legal risks of these third-party tools, e.g. provider terms that allow training on or retaining submitted data, data residency, and IP/licence exposure of the outputs.

rows.why: The likelihood and size of harm from data leaving through unapproved AI tools, and from outside agents, MCP clients and scrapers reaching the org's systems at machine speed, are assessed and recorded.
The org's sign-in flows, APIs and public systems are tested and watched for abuse by outside agents and scrapers, such as delegated sign-in, high-rate calls and bulk extraction.
Traffic to AI services and automated access by outside agents are logged and attributed to a user or client, and the logs are reviewed, so unapproved use can be traced.
Data sent to unapproved AI tools and services is inspected, so the exposure of personal and sensitive data through them is measured.
New unapproved AI use, including AI features switched on in existing software and new outside agent traffic, is detected on an ongoing basis rather than found once.
Data leaked through an unapproved AI tool, or abuse by an outside agent, is reported, responded to, recovered from and recorded as an incident.
Unapproved AI tools, agents and MCP components that are found are removed, quarantined or switched off, with someone responsible for doing it.

Controls are applied to outside AI: unapproved AI services and extensions are blocked or filtered at DNS, web and DLP, and outside agents and MCP clients reaching the org must authenticate and are limited to granted access.

A shadow-AI data leak or outside-agent abuse is communicated to the people whose data was affected, to the AI provider (for example to request deletion) and to other relevant parties, and the communication is documented.
The prompts, pasted text and files sent to each model are traced to where they go, including external providers and the log stores that keep them.
People who send prompts and files to the model are trained on what data may and may not be entered and into which approved tools.
Provider terms and contracts are reviewed for whether the provider keeps, reuses or trains on the prompts and files the organisation sends.
Prompts and responses are logged with who sent them and when, and the logs are kept and reviewed so use of the model can be traced.
Prompts, uploaded files and prompt logs are examined in use for personal or sensitive data being sent to the model or exposed through the logs.

Sensitive input is classified, minimised or redacted before it reaches the model, blocked from unapproved AI services, encrypted, and prompt logs have restricted access, set retention and secure disposal.
Provider-side settings for retention and reuse of submitted prompts and files are applied and regularly checked, with provider telemetry monitored.
Leaks of sensitive data through prompts, files or prompt logs are reported, responded to with the provider where needed, recorded and reviewed.
The knowledge limits of the AI's answers, the uses outside them, and how people and systems downstream may use and must oversee those answers are documented.
rows.review_reason: The why's second half (how people and systems downstream must oversee the answers) repeats MAP 3.5's check (where a person must review an answer and how that oversight works), so both rows would produce the same oversight question; keep MAP 2.2 to the answers' knowledge limits and the uses inside and outside them, and leave oversight to MAP 3.5.

rows.why: The cost, likelihood and magnitude of a wrong or steered answer turning into a wrong decision or action are examined and documented against the risk tolerance.
The decisions and actions where a person must review an AI answer before it is trusted are identified, and that oversight is defined and checked in practice.
The test sets, metrics and tools used to evaluate answer accuracy, consistency and resistance to steering are documented, so the evaluation can be repeated.
Answer quality is monitored in production for wrong answers, inconsistent answers to the same question and drift over time.
Answers are shown to be accurate and consistent under conditions like the deployment setting, including the rate of made-up facts, and the limits beyond which they are not reliable are documented.
The AI is tested for unsafe answers and for failing safely (declining or flagging) when asked beyond its knowledge limits.
Answers are tested for being steered by an attacker through prompt injection in user input or retrieved content, jailbreaks and poisoned answers, and the results are documented.
Answers are logged with the input, model version and who received them, so a wrong decision can be traced back to the answer that caused it.
Users can see how an answer was reached (for example its sources or confidence), so it is interpreted in context rather than trusted blindly.
Users can report wrong or suspicious answers and challenge outcomes based on them, and those reports feed the answer quality metrics.
The remaining risk of wrong answers is documented and disclosed to the people and systems that use them, with known limitations and warnings.
Controls limit what answers can do: output guardrails and business rules, and separation of system instructions from untrusted input and retrieved content.
There are thresholds and named people to switch off or bypass the AI when its answers are wrong or steered beyond what is acceptable.
After deployment, changes to prompts, models or retrieved content are reviewed and the answers re-tested for accuracy and steering before the change goes into production.
Incidents where a wrong or steered answer led to a wrong decision or action, or a new way of steering answers is found, are reported, responded to, recovered from and reviewed.
The upstream sources the tuning and evaluation data depend on, including production feedback and logs reused for tuning, are documented with how that data flows into the sets.
How training, tuning and evaluation sets and the test harness are collected and selected (representativeness, suitability, construct validity) is identified and documented.
Third-party and open datasets used for training, tuning or evaluation are inventoried with their source, licence and the rights to use them, so infringement risks are mapped.
The internal controls for the tuning and evaluation sets, including review of acquired data for bias, privacy and security problems, are identified and documented.
rows.review_reason: Repeats other rows in different words: documenting the controls on the sets is what MANAGE 2.2 checks is done in practice, and reviewing acquired data for bias, privacy and security repeats MEASURE 2.11, MEASURE 2.10 and MEASURE 2.7 (and MANAGE 3.1 for third-party data); it adds no separate check for this area.

rows.why: The test and evaluation sets, the harness test cases, the metrics and the tools used are documented and versioned, for example with data sheets.

Evaluation and tuning sets are checked for representativeness of the real population (including disaggregated groups) and human-subject, consent, privacy and IP requirements are met when the data is collected.
Evaluation and test sets are kept separate from training and tuning data so that measured validity and reliability are not inflated by leakage.
The training, tuning and evaluation data and the harness are tested for poisoning and tampering, for example by integrity checks against known-good versions.
Changes to datasets, evaluation sets and the harness are logged with who made them, so tampering to hide failures can be traced and accounted for.
Sensitive or personal data in training sets and in feedback reused for tuning is identified, classified and access-controlled, and its privacy risk examined.
The training, tuning and evaluation sets are evaluated for bias across and within the groups they represent, with fairness metrics applied and the results documented.
The evaluation sets and harness are themselves reviewed for whether they still catch errors and risks, so a weakened or stale harness does not hide failures.
Data controls are applied to the training, tuning and evaluation data: minimisation, access granted by need, encryption at rest and separation of who may change the data from who promotes models.
When poisoning or tampering of the data or harness is found, a response procedure is followed and clean, backed-up versions of the datasets and evaluation sets are restored.
Third-party datasets used for tuning or evaluation are monitored over time for licence, provenance and quality changes, and risk controls on them are applied and documented.
Modifications to tuning data, such as deletion or rectification requests for feedback and logs reused for tuning, are tracked and carried out with retention and disposal applied.
Incidents and errors involving the datasets or harness are recorded and reviewed with the version history of the data changes, and communicated to the affected AI actors.
The base models, fine-tuned versions, weights and system prompts that make up the model are inventoried with source, version and licence, so ownership and third-party IP or licence limits are known.
The controls protecting each model component (weight storage, model registry, prompt and configuration stores, serving API) are identified and documented, with where each is held.
The test sets, metrics and evaluation harness used to evaluate each model version before release are documented and kept with that version.
The deployed model is monitored in production for behaviour drifting from release testing, unexpected version changes and query patterns that suggest extraction through the API.
Each model version is shown to be valid and reliable (accurate and consistent) for its operating conditions before release, with the limits of its generalisation documented.
The model's resistance to theft, tampering and extraction through its API is tested (for example by red-teaming) and the results and countermeasures are documented.
Access to weights and the model registry, changes to versions, system prompts and configurations, and API use of the model are logged with identity, so theft or tampering can be traced.

Weights, fine-tuned versions and system prompts are protected by least-privilege access, MFA for registry administration, encryption at rest, separation of duties for promotion, and API countermeasures such as throttling against extraction.
Suspected model theft, extraction attempts or tampering with a version are reported and handled under an incident response procedure that covers these scenarios.
A tampered or compromised model version can be withdrawn and rolled back to a protected, integrity-checked known-good version, with set thresholds and owners for doing so.

Third-party pre-trained base models used for fine-tuning are monitored as part of regular model maintenance for tampered or backdoored weights, upstream withdrawals, vulnerabilities and licence changes, and are replaced or retired when they exceed risk tolerance.

Model theft, extraction or tampering incidents are communicated to the relevant AI actors (model owners, downstream users of the affected version, the provider of a base model), and their tracking, response and recovery are documented and reviewed after the event.
The stores the AI retrieves from (vector databases, knowledge graphs, document corpora) are identified with what each holds, where it flows and which AI systems depend on it.
Third-party and licensed content loaded into the retrieval stores is identified, with its source and any rights or licence limits on serving it through the AI.
The controls on each retrieval store are identified and documented, including how its content is classified and who is meant to be able to see it through the AI.
The likelihood and harm of the store's content leaking, being copied out or being poisoned through the AI are assessed against how sensitive that content is.
Retrieval in production is monitored for unexpected changes to store content and for anomalous query patterns that suggest poisoning or bulk extraction.
Retrieval is security tested, for example by red teaming, for permission bypass, poisoned content changing answers and data being exfiltrated through the AI.
Retrieval from the stores is logged with the identity of the requester and the content returned, so access to the data through the AI can be traced and reviewed.
Personal and sensitive information in the retrieval stores is identified and its disclosure through AI answers is checked and monitored.
Controls are applied to the stores: retrieval honours the asking user's permissions, write access is restricted against poisoning, and content is minimised, encrypted and segmented by sensitivity.
A store or source found leaking or poisoned can be disconnected from retrieval, with someone assigned to do it and thresholds that trigger it.
Changes to store content are tracked after deployment, including deletion and rectification requests, retention and secure disposal of embeddings and indexed content.
Incidents such as data leaking through the AI or poisoned store content are reported, responded to, recovered from and recorded, with a review of the affected sources.
The connections each tool or MCP server gives the AI to systems, data and outside networks are documented with their trust boundaries, so it is known what the AI can reach through them.
Tool actions that need a human to confirm them (writes, deletions, payments, sending data out) are identified and the confirmation step is defined.

The MCP servers and tools the AI can call, hosted inside or used from outside, are inventoried with who runs them and their declared capabilities, and the technology and legal risks of each outside server or tool provider (terms of service, licences, data rights, support and release practices) are reviewed and documented.
Controls for each tool and MCP server, such as allowlisting approved servers and classifying outside servers by what they can reach, are identified and documented before the AI uses them.
Threat modelling records how likely and how harmful misuse of each tool is, such as the AI acting with borrowed user permissions or a poisoned outside server, and is repeated when tools change.

Tool controls are regularly reassessed, such as granted OAuth scopes and roles reviewed against actual tool use, and metrics on third-party tools and servers are tracked and updated when they fall short.
Tool use in production is monitored for anomalies, unapproved new capabilities and unexpected outbound calls, and the logs are reviewed.
Tools and MCP servers are security tested, including adversarial prompt and tool poisoning tests and checks that authorisation is enforced on every call.
Tool calls are logged with the user and client identity and credentials used, centralised and retained, including logs from outside servers, so every action the AI takes can be traced.
The personal and sensitive data each tool or MCP server can read or send, including data passed to outside servers with borrowed user permissions, is examined and documented for privacy risk.

Tool access is granted through a defined process with least privilege scopes, strong authentication and separate credentials, and outside and non-production servers are kept apart from production systems.
A newly found vulnerability or risk in a tool, MCP server or its dependencies is triaged by severity, fixed and its root cause analysed.
A tool or MCP server can be disabled quickly by named people, with its tokens and sessions revoked and its data flows stopped.
Outside MCP servers and tool providers are held to contract security requirements, assessed and monitored for changes in version, capabilities and authorisation behaviour.
Tool incidents such as unauthorised invocations, compromised servers or stolen tokens are reported, contained, recorded, reviewed afterwards and communicated to server operators and affected parties.
Each agent's reach is documented: the tools, systems, data and external networks it can act on, its knowledge limits, and where humans oversee its output.
rows.review_reason: Repeats other rows in different words: 'the tools, systems, data and networks it can act on' is the MAP 3.3 scope check and 'where humans oversee its output' is the MAP 3.5 oversight check; narrow it to the agent's documented knowledge limits and how its outputs and actions are relied on downstream.

rows.why: The scope of each agent's deployment is set: which processes, systems and types of action it is allowed into at all and which are out of bounds.
Agent actions that need a human in the loop (irreversible changes, high-value steps, long action chains) are identified and the approval or review step is defined.
The agent's components and suppliers (orchestration framework, LLM, tools, MCP clients and servers, memory stores) are identified with their third-party risks.
Internal controls on the agent's components are identified, such as allowlisted frameworks, libraries, tools and scripts the agent may run.
The likelihood and magnitude of agent harms (prompt injection triggering actions, tool abuse, runaway chains, irreversible changes) are assessed, for example through threat modelling.
Agent behaviour in production is monitored for anomalies such as unexpected tool calls, decision paths, rate or cost spikes, with alert thresholds.
Agents are shown to be valid and reliable before and during use, completing their action chains correctly within documented operating conditions and limits.
Agents are tested to fail safely under stress and beyond their limits, including loop detection and circuit breakers that stop runaway or harmful action chains.
Agent security is tested through red teaming and penetration tests covering direct and indirect prompt injection, tool abuse, memory poisoning and sandbox breakout.
Agent actions are logged end to end (tool calls, data access, authorisation decisions, commands, human overrides) so each action can be traced to the agent identity and reviewed.
Agents run with their own least-privilege identities and capability-bound credentials, and business rules restrict which actions they can take without approval.
rows.review_reason: Missing MANAGE 4.1: nothing checks that, in operation, an agent's actions can be overridden by a human and its irreversible or chained changes rolled back or recovered, with changes to the agent's tools, prompts and permissions put through change management.

rows.why: Agent-specific incidents such as a manipulated or misbehaving agent are responded to and recovered from using playbooks and named responders.
rows.review_reason: Missing MANAGE 4.1: nothing checks that, in operation, an agent's actions can be overridden by a human and its irreversible or chained changes rolled back or recovered, with changes to the agent's tools, prompts and permissions put through change management.

rows.why: An agent can be halted or disengaged when it acts outside its intended use, with thresholds that trigger it, owners who do it, and its credentials revoked.
rows.review_reason: Missing MANAGE 4.1: nothing checks that, in operation, an agent's actions can be overridden by a human and its irreversible or chained changes rolled back or recovered, with changes to the agent's tools, prompts and permissions put through change management.

rows.why: Third-party agent frameworks, tools and platforms are monitored and kept on supported, trusted versions, with risk controls applied to them.
rows.review_reason: Missing MANAGE 4.1: nothing checks that, in operation, an agent's actions can be overridden by a human and its irreversible or chained changes rolled back or recovered, with changes to the agent's tools, prompts and permissions put through change management.

rows.why: Agent misbehaviour and incidents are reported, tracked and reviewed for root cause, and communicated to affected parties and tool or model vendors.
rows.review_reason: Missing MANAGE 4.1: nothing checks that, in operation, an agent's actions can be overridden by a human and its irreversible or chained changes rolled back or recovered, with changes to the agent's tools, prompts and permissions put through change management.

rows.why: The hosting environment's connections and dependencies (serving endpoints, model registry, secret stores, external networks and the internet) are documented, so what the hosted model can reach and what depends on it is known.
The cost of a hosting failure (outage of serving endpoints, compromise of GPUs or the registry, compute or cost abuse) is examined and compared with the organisation's risk tolerance.
The servers, GPUs, model registry, serving runtimes, drivers and third-party hosting software are inventoried with their source and support, and unapproved hosting environments are found.
The hosting infrastructure is monitored in production for intrusion, abnormal traffic, unexpected usage or compute spikes and availability, with alerts raised to the security team.
Serving endpoints and GPU capacity are stress-tested under high load and failure conditions, so the hosting is shown to degrade or fail safely rather than go down or run up unbounded cost.
The hosting environment and its exposed endpoints are regularly scanned and tested for vulnerabilities and attack, and the results are recorded.

Access to and changes on the hosting (inference traffic, registry and deployment events, administrative and secret use) are logged, time-synchronised, centralised and retained so actions can be traced.

The hosting is hardened in practice: secure configuration, host firewalls, network isolation, authenticated gateways and throttling on endpoints, scoped secrets and keys, and only approved software and libraries running.
When the hosting is compromised or goes down, an incident response procedure is followed and models, registry state and configuration are recovered from protected, tested backups.
Named people can take a serving endpoint offline, revoke its keys, roll back to a known-good version or fail over to a backup, and evidence is preserved when they do.
Third-party hosting software (serving frameworks, GPU drivers, container images, operating systems) is tracked for updates and patched or remediated by risk.
rows.review_reason: LLM-7.3 (OS patching of compute hosts) and the 'operating systems' in the why are general host hygiene, not risk from third-party AI resources; MANAGE 3.1 should stay on third-party serving frameworks, runtimes, drivers and images (LLM-7.4), and OS patching belongs with the hardening row (MANAGE 2.2).

rows.why: Hosting incidents and outages are reported, recorded and communicated to the people affected, and each is reviewed after closure with changes to the hosting tracked.

description: AI RMF mapping: per AI area, rows of AI RMF function -> subcategory, CIS safeguards that prove it, impact. Drafted and evaluated by agents (prompts/ai_rmf_mapping_*.md), recorded by record_ai_bank.py mapping, reviewed by a person. Model: AI_RMF_Mapping_Sheet_Design.md.
